newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU, U.S. ready to improve telecoms trade offers.
newsitem.headline: EU, U.S. ready to improve telecoms trade offers.

text.p: The European Union and United States are ready to submit improved offers on telecommunications liberalisation in world trade talks following weekend talks, the European Commission said on Monday.
"That will provide the joint transatlantic leadership which will get the rest of the world, we hope, to improve their telecoms offers," Commission spokesman Peter Guilford told a news briefing.

Guilford said progress was made possible after the EU executive announced during talks with U.S. officials in Chicago that Spain had agreed to open its telecommunications market to competition by late 1998 and to end remaining restrictions on foreign ownership.
"This was the main European hurdle to American progress in the telecoms talks," he said, adding that the United States would shortly announce its own improved offer.

World Trade Organisation (WTO) talks on a world telecoms accord take place this week in Geneva. The pact was originally due to be finalised last April 30, but Washington pulled out at the last minute, saying offers on the table, especially from Asia and Latin America, were not good enough.
Spain had the possibility under EU law to delay fully liberalising its telecoms markets for up to five years beyond the January 1, 1998 deadline agreed by most other EU countries.
But the Commission put pressure on Madrid to renounce that right, arguing that it was a stumbling block to an accord with the United States.

Guilford said the two sides also moved forward on two other issues -- a global trade agreement on information technology products and U.S.-EU "mutual recognition" accords allowing products to be exported without having to be reapproved in each other's market.

EU and U.S. business leaders attending the Chicago talks pushed hard for conclusion of an Information Technology Agreement, which would eliminate tariffs on a range of computer and telecommunications products, at the Singapore WTO ministerial meeting in December.

"That has concentrated the minds," Guilford said. He said the Commission warned, however, that any attempt by the United States or other parties to get exemptions or transition periods for their own industries could cause the deal to unravel.

The two sides also moved made unexpected progress on the major stumbling block in mutual recognitions talks -- Washington's insistence that the Federal Drug Administration have the right to carry out second approvals of European pharmaceutical exports.
The business leaders suggested a formula under which either side may carry out second approvals, but only in narrow circumstances, Guilford said.
The Commission and the U.S. government will define what those circumstances are before the end of January, he said.
